growth_story.headline: After a deep post-Soviet collapse, the Kyrgyz Republic grew unevenly for two decades, then boomed from 2022 on trade, remittances and construction.
growth_story.arc: In 1990–1997, income per person fell by 6.1 percent a year on average, shrinking every year from 1991 to 1995 and by as much as 20.1 percent in 1994. The World Bank dates the bottom of the transition recession to 1995, and growth came back in 1996 and 1997. From 1998 to 2025, growth averaged 3.1 percent a year, but it was uneven: income per person fell in 2002, 2005, 2010 and 2012, years the World Bank links to revolutions and falls in gold output, and it dropped 9.0 percent in 2020 with the pandemic and political turmoil. From 2022 to 2025, growth ran between 7.0 and 9.7 percent a year. The IMF puts this down to bigger trade flows, strong remittance and capital inflows, and a building boom. As a result, the last ten years averaged 3.6 percent against 3.1 in the decade before, and income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025.

threads.title: Transition collapse and slow catch-up
threads.text: Like other former Soviet economies, the country went through a deep recession in the early 1990s that hit bottom in 1995. The World Bank notes that most of those economies then grew faster than the Kyrgyz Republic. In the data, income per person did not pass its 1990 level until 2022.

threads.title: Gold and political upheaval
threads.text: After 1998 growth kept breaking off for a year at a time. The World Bank ties these dips to swings in gold output, which grew in importance after the Kumtor mine opened in 1997, and to the country's revolutions and changes of government.

threads.title: A slowdown, then the 2020 shock
threads.text: Growth was already slowing in the late 2010s, with income per person growing between 1.5 and 2.6 percent a year from 2016 to 2019. In 2020 the pandemic and political turmoil came together, remittances fell, and income per person dropped 9.0 percent.

threads.title: Remittances and gold still matter
threads.text: Since the 2000s, many workers have gone abroad for jobs, mostly to Russia, and the money they send home has helped cut poverty, especially among the poorest households. The World Bank still counts gold exports and remittances among the economy's main supports.

threads.text: Since 2022, trade flows through the country have grown fast, alongside strong inflows of remittances and capital and a building boom. The IMF sees a possible reversal of re-export trade as a risk, and the World Bank sees tighter sanctions on Russia as a risk to trade.

since_last_year.text: The boom continued: income per person grew 9.3 percent in 2025. The World Bank says that more recently, public and private investment has done more of the work, and the IMF expects growth to ease as re-export trade levels off. Prices rose faster again after fuel supplies from Russia were disrupted in May 2026.

growth_story.tension: A World Bank report from 2023 called the growth model failing, after growth slowed in the late 2010s, and a 2020 report described growth as modest and volatile. The data show something better: growth over the last ten years (3.6 percent a year) beat the decade before (3.1), and income per person is at its peak. Almost all of that gain comes from 2022–2025, after those reports were written. The data also show a current account deficit of 36.6 percent of GDP in 2024. The World Bank notes that re-exports are under-reported in the official figures and show up instead under errors and omissions, so part of the recorded gap reflects trade that is not counted.
